# About this edition {.unnumbered}

This is a work-in-progress 2026 revised edition of David MacKay's
*Sustainable Energy — Without the Hot Air* (2008), rebuilt with
[Quarto](https://quarto.org) from the markdown source preserved by the
[Life Itself climate project](https://github.com/life-itself/climate).

MacKay's text is reproduced unchanged. Most of his figures have been replaced by versions carrying the same series to the present; where a figure of his is retained, or replaced, the caption says so. New material added in
this revision is marked in the chapter where it appears, and several chapters are
new in their entirety. The table below is the authoritative list of them.

## Latest changes

Last updated **31 August 2026**. The complete history is in the
[repository](https://github.com/oluies/climate/commits/main).

| Date | What changed |
|---|---|
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 26 gains the Swedish case: day-ahead arbitrage does not cover a battery's capital even with 17% of hours under €10, while the reserve markets do — and they pay per megawatt of availability, so nothing in them rewards a fifth hour of storage. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figure 1.6 replaces MacKay's two population graphs. Britain multiplied six-fold while its coal did, then grew 69% in the 125 years since; the world went the other way. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: MacKay's four rectangle diagrams are numbered 1.7 to 1.10, so his own construction can be referred to and it is visible which new figure updates which. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figure 1.8 adds emissions per person over time. China passed the world average in 2006, the EU in 2013 and the UK in 2014, while every wealthy bloc roughly halved and the world average went from 4.3 to 4.7. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figure 1.8 adds cumulative emissions. MacKay's claim that Britain is second only to the United States among historical emitters per person is still true — 1 158 tonnes a head against 1 259 — and is the one thing in the chapter that has not moved. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figure 1.7 redraws MacKay's rectangle construction for 2000 and 2023. China goes from the wide, low block he describes to the largest area on the chart, taller than Japan; the United States falls from 26 tonnes a head to 18. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1 rebuilt: MacKay's superseded figures are replaced rather than duplicated, and figures 1.8 and 1.9 are new — the world is 1% above its 2007 emissions per person on paths that required a steep fall, and a third of all greenhouse gases now come from electricity and heat. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figures 1.3a, 1.4a and 1.5a. The energy gap closed more by demand falling a quarter than by wind rising; CO₂ is 426 ppm against the 383 where MacKay's chart ends; and the early coal history redrawn legibly. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figure 1.6a carries the coal chart to 2025. British coal peaked in 1913 and produced 1 TWh last year; world production is five and a half times its 1913 level and set its record in the 2020s. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1: figure 1.2a carries MacKay's North Sea chart forward to 2025. Production is down 57% from its 2000 peak, Britain's own share down 77%, while the real price went above anything on his original. |
| 31 August 2026 | Chapter 1 picks up the security-of-supply motivation MacKay drops: three-fifths of world oil comes from autocracies, Sweden buys 96% of its crude from democracies, and fungibility means that does not help. Chapter N contrasts it with uranium. |
| 30 August 2026 | Chapter 26: a cheaper cell arrives with a tax advantage behind it, and changes nothing about duration — with the sodium cost claim checked against the lithium price it is measured against. |
| 28 August 2026 | Chapter 31 gains the carbon cost of a war — four years of the war in Ukraine counted in tonnes, what removing them would cost, and the peacetime military emissions no inventory records; chapter 17 points to it. |
| 21 August 2026 | Chapter 6 gains a check on solar power per unit area from Chinese utility-scale data, which reaches Cleve Hill's figure by an independent route; chapter L the land totals that go with it; chapter 31 a daily carbon dioxide series behind the "nine seconds" comparison. |
| 21 August 2026 | Chapter 11a gains the electricity cost of a single AI answer, the land a data-centre campus stands on, who pays for its winning bid, and what generates its power. |
| 20 August 2026 | Chapter 28a: two claims about flexibility narrowed to what the study behind them supports. |
| 19 August 2026 | Chapter 28a: the German flexibility study's own figures moved into the text. |
| 17 August 2026 | Chapter 28a argues the agency problem from the mechanism rather than a political slogan. Figure scripts declare their dependencies and run under uv. |
| 16–17 August 2026 | Chapter L: a third way of counting emissions and what it does to Sweden, and corrections to the carbon explorer instructions. |
| 15–16 August 2026 | Chapter 31: drained peat, and why filling the ditches in does not undo it. |

## New chapters

Each of these says so at the top, and none of them is MacKay's writing.

| Chapter | What it is for | Added |
|---|---|---|
| [**11a** *The machines behind the screen*](chapters/chap11a.md) | Data centres, from MacKay's 0.4 kWh/d footnote about servers to a load that outbids industry and housing for a grid connection. | 3 August 2026 |
| [**28a** *The value of renewable energy as it scales*](chapters/chap-value-of-renewables.md) | What happens to the economic value of renewable electricity as it grows to the scale the balance sheet calls for. | 30 July 2026 |
| [**L** *The world in 2025*](chapters/chapL.md) | MacKay's stock-taking redone for the most recent complete year. | 1 August 2026 |
| [**M** *Energy return on investment*](chapters/chapM.md) | The question chapter 3 asks and then declines to answer properly. | 2 August 2026 |
| [**N** *Peak oil, peak gas, peak uranium*](chapters/chapN.md) | Chapter 23's Jevons calculation carried forward to the fuels it now matters for. | 2 August 2026 |
| [**O** *The hydrogen ladder*](chapters/chapO.md) | Which uses of hydrogen are worth the electricity they cost, ranked. | 9 August 2026 |
